front: Le 14 juillet, on célèbre la prise de la Bastille.
pronunciation: [luh kah-torz zhwee-YEH, ohn say-lebr lah preez duh lah bas-TEEY]
back: On 14 July, the storming of the Bastille is celebrated.
context: The national holiday commemorates 14 July 1789. English speakers call it Bastille Day; the French say 'le 14 Juillet' or 'la fête nationale'.

front: Le défilé militaire descend les Champs-Élysées.
pronunciation: [luh day-fee-lay mee-lee-TEHR day-sahn lay shahn zay-lee-ZAY]
back: The military parade goes down the Champs-Élysées.
context: Followed in the evening by fireworks and 'bals des pompiers' (firefighters' dances).

front: La Fête de la musique a lieu le 21 juin.
pronunciation: [lah fet duh lah mü-ZEEK ah lyuh luh van tay an ZHWAN]
back: The Music Festival takes place on 21 June.
context: Created in France in 1982: free concerts in the streets on the longest day of the year.

front: À l'Épiphanie, on mange la galette des rois.
pronunciation: [ah lay-pee-fah-NEE, ohn mahnzh lah gah-let day RWAH]
back: At Epiphany, we eat the kings' cake.
context: Whoever finds 'la fève' (the small charm) becomes king or queen for the day and wears the paper crown.

front: Pour la Chandeleur, on fait des crêpes.
pronunciation: [poor lah shahn-duh-LUHR, ohn feh day KREP]
back: For Candlemas, we make crêpes.
context: On 2 February. Tradition says you flip a crêpe holding a coin for prosperity.

front: Le premier mai, on offre du muguet.
pronunciation: [luh pruh-myay MEH, ohn noh-fruh dü mü-GEH]
back: On 1 May, people give lily of the valley.
context: A lucky charm on Labour Day; anyone may sell it in the street that day.

front: Le poisson d'avril est une tradition très ancienne.
pronunciation: [luh pwah-sohn dah-VREEL eh tün trah-dee-syohn treh zahn-SYEN]
back: April Fool's is a very old tradition.
context: Children stick paper fish on people's backs on 1 April.

front: Le réveillon de Noël se passe en famille.
pronunciation: [luh ray-veh-yohn duh noh-EL suh pas ahn fah-MEE]
back: Christmas Eve dinner is spent with family.
context: 'Le réveillon' = the festive late dinner on 24 and 31 December.

front: Au Nouvel An, on s'embrasse sous le gui à minuit.
pronunciation: [oh noo-vel AHN, ohn sahm-bras soo luh GEE ah mee-NWEE]
back: At New Year, people kiss under the mistletoe at midnight.
context: In France, mistletoe is a New Year tradition rather than a Christmas one.

front: On se souhaite la bonne année jusqu'à la fin janvier.
pronunciation: [ohn suh sweht lah bun ah-NAY zhüs-kah lah fan zhahn-VYAY]
back: People wish each other a happy new year until the end of January.
context: 'Meilleurs vœux !' = best wishes. Saying it in February is too late!

front: La Toussaint, on fleurit les tombes avec des chrysanthèmes.
pronunciation: [lah too-SAN, ohn fluh-ree lay tohmb ah-vek day kree-zahn-TEM]
back: On All Saints' Day, people decorate graves with chrysanthemums.
context: On 1 November. Never offer chrysanthemums as a gift: they're associated with the dead.

front: Chaque région a ses traditions et son identité.
pronunciation: [shak ray-zhyohn ah say trah-dee-SYOHN ay sohn nee-dahn-tee-TAY]
back: Each region has its own traditions and identity.
context: France is very centralized, but regional identities remain strong.

front: En Bretagne, on danse lors des fest-noz.
pronunciation: [ahn bruh-TAN-yuh, ohn dahns lor day fest-NOHZ]
back: In Brittany, people dance at fest-noz.
context: 'Fest-noz' (Breton, 'night festival') = traditional dance gatherings, listed by UNESCO.

front: Le breton est une langue celtique encore parlée aujourd'hui.
pronunciation: [luh bruh-TOHN eh tün lahng sel-TEEK ahn-kor par-lay oh-zhoor-DWEE]
back: Breton is a Celtic language still spoken today.
context: France has several regional languages: breton, basque, occitan, corse, alsacien…

front: Le carnaval de Nice est l'un des plus célèbres au monde.
pronunciation: [luh kar-nah-vahl duh NEES eh lan day plü say-leh-bruh oh MOHND]
back: The Nice Carnival is one of the most famous in the world.
context: Held in February, with the famous 'bataille de fleurs' (flower battle).

front: La fête du citron a lieu chaque année à Menton.
pronunciation: [lah fet dü see-TROHN ah lyuh shak ah-nay ah mahn-TOHN]
back: The Lemon Festival takes place every year in Menton.
context: Giant sculptures made of citrus fruit on the Riviera.

front: En Alsace, les marchés de Noël sont une institution.
pronunciation: [ahn nal-ZAS, lay mar-shay duh noh-EL sohn tün an-stee-tü-SYOHN]
back: In Alsace, Christmas markets are an institution.
context: With mulled wine ('vin chaud') and gingerbread ('pain d'épices').

front: Dans le Sud-Ouest, les fêtes de Bayonne attirent un million de visiteurs.
pronunciation: [dahn luh sü-DWEST, lay fet duh bah-YON ah-teer an mee-lyohn duh vee-zee-TUHR]
back: In the southwest, the Bayonne festival draws a million visitors.
context: Everyone dresses in white with a red scarf.

front: La pétanque est un jeu typique du Sud.
pronunciation: [lah pay-TAHNK eh tan zhuh tee-peek dü SÜD]
back: Pétanque is a typical game from the south.
context: Played with metal balls ('les boules') aiming at a small wooden ball ('le cochonnet').

front: Le Tour de France passe chaque juillet par des centaines de villages.
pronunciation: [luh toor duh FRAHNS pas shak zhwee-YEH par day sahn-ten duh vee-LAHZH]
back: Every July, the Tour de France passes through hundreds of villages.
context: Created in 1903, it's a huge popular festival as much as a race.

front: Les Journées européennes du patrimoine attirent des millions de curieux.
pronunciation: [lay zhoor-nay zuh-roh-pay-en dü pah-tree-MWAHN ah-teer day mee-lyohn duh kü-RYUH]
back: European Heritage Days attract millions of curious visitors.
context: Each September, the Élysée Palace and many other buildings open their doors.

front: Le Beaujolais nouveau est arrivé !
pronunciation: [luh boh-zhoh-leh noo-voh eh tah-ree-VAY]
back: The Beaujolais nouveau has arrived!
context: Released on the third Thursday of November, a marketing tradition since the 1950s–70s.

front: Au Moyen Âge, les troubadours chantaient l'amour courtois.
pronunciation: [oh mwah-yen NAHZH, lay troo-bah-DOOR shahn-teh lah-moor koor-TWAH]
back: In the Middle Ages, troubadours sang of courtly love.
context: Troubadours wrote in Occitan, the language of the south.

front: Le folklore régional connaît un renouveau chez les jeunes.
pronunciation: [luh folk-lor ray-zhyoh-NAL koh-neh tan ruh-noo-VOH shay lay ZHUHN]
back: Regional folklore is enjoying a revival among young people.
context: 'Un renouveau' = a revival.

front: La légende raconte qu'une fée vivait dans cette forêt.
pronunciation: [lah lay-zhahnd rah-kohnt kün FAY vee-veh dahn set foh-REH]
back: Legend has it that a fairy lived in this forest.
context: Brittany's Brocéliande forest is linked to the legends of King Arthur and Merlin.

front: En Provence, on prépare treize desserts pour Noël.
pronunciation: [ahn proh-VAHNS, ohn pray-par trez deh-SEHR poor noh-EL]
back: In Provence, people prepare thirteen desserts for Christmas.
context: Representing Jesus and the twelve apostles.

front: Les santons de Provence décorent les crèches.
pronunciation: [lay sahn-TOHN duh proh-VAHNS day-kor lay KRESH]
back: Provençal santons decorate nativity scenes.
context: 'Les santons' = small clay figurines, a Provençal craft tradition.

front: À Lyon, la Fête des Lumières illumine la ville chaque décembre.
pronunciation: [ah lee-OHN, lah fet day lü-MYEHR ee-lü-meen lah veel shak day-SAHM-bruh]
back: In Lyon, the Festival of Lights lights up the city every December.
context: Around 8 December, residents put candles on their windowsills.

front: La Corse a une culture et une langue très marquées.
pronunciation: [lah KORS ah ün kül-tür ay ün lahng treh mar-KAY]
back: Corsica has a very distinctive culture and language.
context: 'Marqué' = pronounced, distinctive.

front: Les Antilles fêtent le carnaval avec beaucoup d'énergie.
pronunciation: [lay zahn-TEEY fet luh kar-nah-VAL ah-vek boh-koo day-nehr-ZHEE]
back: The French Caribbean celebrates carnival with great energy.
context: Guadeloupe and Martinique are overseas departments with Creole culture.

front: Le créole est parlé en Martinique, en Guadeloupe et à La Réunion.
pronunciation: [luh kray-OL eh par-LAY ahn mar-tee-NEEK, ahn gwah-duh-LOOP ay ah lah ray-ü-NYOHN]
back: Creole is spoken in Martinique, Guadeloupe and Réunion.
context: French-based Creoles are distinct languages.

front: Cette tradition remonte au dix-neuvième siècle.
pronunciation: [set trah-dee-syohn ruh-mohnt oh deez-nuh-vyem SYEH-kluh]
back: This tradition dates back to the 19th century.
context: 'Remonter à' = to date back to.

front: Les jeunes perpétuent les coutumes de leurs grands-parents.
pronunciation: [lay zhuhn pehr-pay-tü lay koo-tüm duh luhr grahn-pah-RAHN]
back: Young people carry on their grandparents' customs.
context: 'Perpétuer' = to perpetuate. 'Une coutume' = a custom.

front: Le muguet porte bonheur, paraît-il.
pronunciation: [luh mü-geh port boh-NUHR, pah-reh-TEEL]
back: Lily of the valley brings good luck, apparently.
context: 'Porter bonheur' = to bring luck. 'Paraît-il' = apparently (inverted).

front: Les Français sont très attachés à leurs jours fériés.
pronunciation: [lay frahn-SEH sohn treh zah-tah-shay ah luhr zhoor fay-RYAY]
back: French people are very attached to their public holidays.
context: France has 11 public holidays ('jours fériés').

front: Quand un jour férié tombe un jeudi, on fait souvent le pont.
pronunciation: [kahn tan zhoor fay-ryay tohmb an zhuh-DEE, ohn feh soo-vahn luh POHN]
back: When a public holiday falls on a Thursday, people often take Friday off too.
context: 'Faire le pont' (make the bridge) = take the day between a holiday and the weekend.

front: Mai est le mois des ponts.
pronunciation: [MEH eh luh mwah day POHN]
back: May is the month of long weekends.
context: With 1 May, 8 May, Ascension and sometimes Pentecost Monday.

front: Le 11 novembre commémore l'armistice de 1918.
pronunciation: [luh ohnz noh-VAHM-bruh koh-may-mor lar-mees-TEES duh meel nuhf sahn dee-ZWEET]
back: 11 November commemorates the 1918 Armistice.
context: Every village has a 'monument aux morts' (war memorial).

front: La fête des voisins rassemble les habitants d'un même immeuble.
pronunciation: [lah fet day vwah-ZAN rah-sahm-bluh lay zah-bee-tahn dan mem ee-MUH-bluh]
back: Neighbors' Day brings together the residents of a building.
context: Created in Paris in 1999 to fight urban isolation.

front: Le bal du 14 juillet est un moment de convivialité.
pronunciation: [luh bal dü kah-torz zhwee-YEH eh tan moh-mahn duh kohn-vee-vyah-lee-TAY]
back: The 14 July dance is a moment of friendliness and togetherness.
context: 'La convivialité' = conviviality, a key French social value.

front: Ce festival met à l'honneur les cultures du monde entier.
pronunciation: [suh fes-tee-VAL meh tah loh-NUHR lay kül-tür dü mohnd ahn-TYAY]
back: This festival showcases cultures from all over the world.
context: 'Mettre à l'honneur' = to celebrate, showcase.

front: Le festival d'Avignon est le plus grand festival de théâtre au monde.
pronunciation: [luh fes-tee-val dah-vee-NYOHN eh luh plü grahn fes-tee-val duh tay-AH-truh oh MOHND]
back: The Avignon Festival is the largest theater festival in the world.
context: Every July, with its official 'In' and its huge 'Off'.

front: Le festival de Cannes récompense les meilleurs films du monde.
pronunciation: [luh fes-tee-val duh KAN ray-kohm-pahns lay meh-yuhr feelm dü MOHND]
back: The Cannes Film Festival rewards the best films in the world.
context: Its top prize is the Palme d'or.

front: Chaque village organise sa fête patronale.
pronunciation: [shak vee-lahzh or-gah-neez sah fet pah-troh-NAL]
back: Every village holds its patron saint's festival.
context: Often with a funfair ('la fête foraine') and a dance.

front: Ces traditions font partie de notre identité.
pronunciation: [say trah-dee-syohn fohn par-tee duh noh-tree-dahn-tee-TAY]
back: These traditions are part of our identity.
context: 'Faire partie de' = to be part of.
